title: Connected nilpotent groups with unipotent centre are unipotent
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups are affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Unipotent means admitting a closed group immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] into some $\mathcal U_{n,k}\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$, $n\geq1$ [def-sc-general-linear-group], where $\mathcal U_{n,k}(A)$ consists of upper triangular matrices with diagonal entries $1$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$. The centre $Z(G)$ is the closed commutative subgroup of [lem-sfb-affine-group-centre-base-change]: its $A$-points commute with all $G(A^{\prime})$ after every commutative $A$-algebra extension $A^{\prime}$. Nilpotent means admitting a finite series $G=G_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq G_s=1$ of closed normal subgroup schemes with $[G(A),G_i(A)]\subseteq G_{i+1}(A)$ for all commutative $k$-algebras $A$ and all $i<s$. Assume $G$ is connected [def-weil-connected-scheme] and nilpotent. If $Z(G)$ is unipotent, then $G$ is unipotent. No smoothness or perfectness is assumed.

source.place: Lemma 16.46, printed pp.340–341; Theorem 14.5 and Corollary 14.9, pp.281–282, for the closed unitriangular realization over k.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-unipotence-field-extension] we may pass to an algebraic closure $K$ of $k$: the given central series remains a central series on all $K$-algebras, and [lem-sfb-affine-group-centre-base-change] identifies $Z(G_K)$ with $Z(G)_K$. Connectedness is preserved because the identity is a $k$-point, by [lem-sbc-connected-rational-point-geometrically-connected]. Hence assume $k$ algebraically closed. Induct on a bound $s$ for the length of the given central series, for all connected affine groups with unipotent centre. If $s=0$, $G=1$, and if $s=1$, $G=Z(G)$, so the assertion holds. The trivial group embeds in $\mathcal U_1$.

source.place: Lemma 16.46, first paragraph; Corollary 14.9, p.282. Agent repair: use central-series length instead of dimension.

proof.text: For $s\geq2$ put $Z=Z(G)$ and form $H=G/Z$ by [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. It is connected, since $G$ is geometrically connected and the quotient lemma preserves this property. It has a central series of length at most $s-1$: $G_{s-1}\subseteq Z$, and the scheme-theoretic images of $G_i$ in $H$ satisfy the same commutator inclusions and end in $1$. These images exist by [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization]; the identities descend because quotient elements lift fppf locally. Choose the largest multiplicative-type subgroup $D=Z(H)_s$ by [lem-sfb-commutative-multiplicative-part], and let $N$ be its inverse image in $G$. Since $D\subseteq Z(H)$ is central, it is normal in $H$, so the quotient lemma gives $N/Z\simeq D$ and normality of $N$ in $G$.

source.place: Lemma 16.46, p.341: G prime and N. Central-series quotient is the agent-supplied induction bookkeeping.

proof.text: The kernel $Z$ of $N\to D$ is central and $D$ is commutative. Thus $[x,y]\in Z$ and $[xx^{\prime},y]=[x,y][x^{\prime},y]$, $[x,yy^{\prime}]=[x,y][x,y^{\prime}]$. Changing either lift by an element of $Z$ does not change the commutator. The fppf quotient property therefore gives a morphism $b:D\times D\to Z$ which is a homomorphism separately in each variable. For a commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and $d\in D(A)$, $b(d,-):D_A\to Z_A$ is trivial by [lem-sfb-multiplicative-unipotent-base-algebra-vanishing]. Consequently $b=1$ on all algebra-valued points, and $N$ is commutative. Here descent uses precisely the sheaf quotient and local lifting of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], not surjectivity on $k$-points.

source.place: Agent commutator argument using Proposition 15.18, p.312, in place of the nested dimension induction in Lemma 16.46(b).

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-commutative-diagonalizable-unipotent-product] to $N$: write $N=U\times T$ with $U$ unipotent and $T$ diagonalizable. The homomorphism $U\to D$ is trivial by [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial], so $T\to D$ is fppf locally surjective: lift a section to $N$ and take its $T$-component. The inclusion $Z\to N$ has trivial composite to $T$ by [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial], so $Z\subseteq U$ and $T\cap Z=1$. Thus $T\to D$ is an isomorphism of fppf sheaves; also $U\subseteq\ker(N\to D)=Z$, so $U=Z$ and $N=T\times Z$. Every automorphism of $N_A$ preserves $T_A$: its composite $T_A\to N_A\to Z_A$ is trivial by [lem-sfb-multiplicative-unipotent-base-algebra-vanishing], and applying this to the inverse gives equality. Conjugation by $G$ therefore normalizes $T$. Apply [lem-sfb-normal-multiplicative-layers-central] to the connected group $G$ with the normal subgroups $1\subseteq T$ (the trivial group is of multiplicative type, and $\mathrm{id}_T$ represents $T/1$): $T\subseteq Z(G)=Z$. In $N=T\times Z$ the intersection is trivial; hence $T=1$, $D=1$, and $N=Z$.

source.place: Lemma 16.46(b), p.341, commutative splitting, characteristic multiplicative factor and centrality; Theorem 16.13(b), p.328, and Corollary 12.38, p.244, and Lemma 16.43, p.340.

proof.text: Since $D=1$, [lem-sfb-commutative-multiplicative-part] applied to $Z(H)$ says $Z(H)/D=Z(H)$ is unipotent. The induction hypothesis applies to connected $H$ and its central series of length at most $s-1$, so $H$ is unipotent. The exact fppf quotient $1\to Z\to G\to H\to1$ from [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] has unipotent kernel and quotient. By [lem-sfb-unipotent-extension-arbitrary], $G$ is unipotent. Finally [lem-sfb-unipotence-field-extension] descends this conclusion to the original field.

source.place: Lemma 16.46 conclusion, pp.340--341; Corollaries 14.7 and 14.9, p.282; central-series induction as above.
